title: Property alternative requires discipline
full_text:
Alternative structures exist that still allow an SMSF to invest in residential property, but their use requires a strong hands-off approach to avoid breaching superannuation laws, an industry specialist has noted.
Auditors Institute ambassador Graeme Colley said following the restrictions on using a limited recourse borrowing arrangement (LRBA) to purchase residential property that took effect from 10 August, investment via unit trust structures was still on the table.
“Following 10 August, what you need to think about is other ways in which the legislation may work and I suggest if you or your clients are thinking about alternative arrangements, be very careful with it,” Colley said at the institute’s Auditors Day 2026 in Melbourne last week.
“In a simple model you can have an SMSF invested in a unit trust, which will own property and that might be residential property, but there is nothing wrong in doing that.
“If the fund invests with a related party, the latter might borrow and purchase units in that unit trust and the trust might end up not being geared. In those cases [Superannuation Industry (Supervision) Regulation] 13.22C could apply and that will be okay.
“However, you really have to know your client because some can’t help themselves and not put their hands into the unit trust and then they will invest somewhere or they put it in a [non-authorised deposit-taking Institution] bank account and that creates real problems with the underlying ungeared unit trust.
“The reason is because if by their actions they create a geared unit trust, they are limited in those circumstances where you have a 50-50 split between the SMSF and the related-party money because the fund is limited by the 5 per cent in-house asset rule, which is going to be an impairment in those cases.
“Whether the client is only going to leave it at 5 per cent or the value of that property is going to increase, which might increase the value of the fund’s assets so that it breaches the in-house asset rules, is something you are going to get into the client and talk to them if it looks like it’s going to happen in relation to a particular property.
“You really need to work out for some clients whether that alternative is going to work or whether they’re going to make an absolute botch of it.”
author: Jason Spits
